To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
for some nutrients and matrices, the analytical performance was poor.

(1) for some nutrients (Na and vitamins A and C), >20% and for some components (fat, niacin, and vitamin C) >25% of the values reported by contract laboratories for CRMs were unacceptable; (2) for other components (Mg, P, Mn and Se, and vitamins B12 and B6) almost all values were within the expected range; (3) for some nutrients and components, deviations from assigned values varied across materials, indicating that

The Z′-scores for most nutrients in the 259 CRMs were acceptable, but some nutrients (Na folate, dietary fibre, pantothenate, thiamine, tocopherols and carotenoids, MUFA, and PUFA) had unacceptable Z′-scores in >20% of CRMs; and the Z′-scores of the 259 CRMS were not uniform across all nutrients, suggesting analytical problems specific to certain nutrients or matrices.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of reference materials to evaluate measurement methods for food composition analysis, and with the use of such materials for the evaluation of the accuracy of measurement methods used by contract laboratories in the United States.
evaluating the accuracy of contract laboratories’ measurements of nutrients in foods and the quality of the reference materials used for these measurements.
the evaluation of measurement systems for the determination of nutrients in food matrices.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, for most nutrients, the data are not adequate to support a conclusion that a measurement system is acceptable, but for some nutrients, the data suggest that a measurement system may be adequate for the intended purpose.
for some nutrients and some matrices, the performance of the laboratories in the NFNAP is not acceptable.
for many nutrients the data from the NFNAP are not sufficient to support a statement that the measurement system is capable of producing reliable results for the nutrient in question.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the data show that there are many nutrients for which the measurement system is not working well.
for most nutrients and laboratories, most values for the CRM were close enough to the assigned value to be acceptable.
the analytical systems used by contract laboratories are not uniformly adequate for all nutrients and matrices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the NFNAP has identified some nutrients that are problematic in terms of the measurement system and that the NFN AP can serve as an important source for identifying such issues.
for some nutrients, especially those present in foods at low concentration and those that require specialized analysis, the uncertainty in the measurement system is large.
the CRM used in NFNAP are not uniformly suitable for evaluating measurement systems for all nutrients.
